title: Avoiding the Blind Spots of the State Sector
author: Samuel Kammin
summary: Kammin reports on a visit to Lumiar School, a small farm-based school with project-based, multi-age, child-centred teaching, and asks whether it avoids the blind spots of the state system. He starts with a headteacher's story of being told her Reception data was too good, which shows how progress metrics can create perverse incentives. He describes the Mosaic competency curriculum, term-long projects and the dual Tutor and Master staffing model. He then presses on the model's costs: assessment consistency, curricular breadth and coherence across children with different projects, parallel to a Bedales visit. He closes that Lumiar is no perfect answer but a reminder that how school feels to a child matters.
points: Accountability measures of progress can punish strong starting points, and one headteacher left the state sector over it.
Lumiar organises learning around term projects, mixed-age cycles and competencies, with permanent tutors and visiting expert masters.
Personalised competency curricula create hard problems of assessment consistency and coherent knowledge.
Inspectors used to mainstream expectations can misread unfamiliar models, though this is not an argument against scrutiny.
quotes: Because national accountability metrics reward schools for showing steep progress over time, high starting scores in the early years were seen as a liability rather than a triumph.

How do you ensure that learning is assessed consistently? How do you know that children are developing a sufficiently broad and coherent body of knowledge when their projects and interests may differ so radically?
Personalisation may offer an escape from the limitations of a one size fits all curriculum, but unfortunately it brings its own demands for clarity, coherence and consistency
But they do illustrate how easily an unfamiliar model can be judged through the organisational lens and expectations of the conventional mainstream one.
Instead, it is the skills, values and dispositions the children are instilled with that matter most to Lumiar.
Lumiar is not a perfect answer to the problems of mainstream education, nor does it need to be.
This serves as a reminder that how school feels to a child really does matter, even if it isn't everything.
